stories.headline: New bionic hand lets users feel pressure
stories.body: Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. He tried several prosthetic devices over the years. The newest hand connects to nerves in his forearm. It transmits pressure signals so he can feel objects. He can now handle delicate items with his left limb.
stories.aha: You’d expect a prosthetic to only move, but this one restores sensation, changing daily tasks.

stories.headline: Europe relies more on U.S. despite sovereignty promises
stories.body: Europe says it wants economic independence from the United States. In practice, its dependence on U.S. resources has increased. Promises to diversify have not turned into real actions yet. American influence remains strong across European markets. The gap between talk and action widens daily.
stories.aha: Talk of sovereignty masks continued reliance, showing political statements can differ from economic reality.

stories.headline: Solo dining reshapes restaurant industry trends
stories.body: Eating alone is becoming a popular self‑care habit. People spend about two hundred pounds each month on meals. Restaurants adapt menus and spaces for single diners. The trend influences how chefs design portion sizes. Industry analysts note growing revenue from solo customers.
stories.aha: Solo meals are not just personal choice; they drive major changes in how restaurants operate.

rabbit.title: Do AI labels really change how we trust information?
rabbit.body: A German study tested if labeling text as AI‑generated affects ratings. Participants read nutrition advice marked as AI‑generated or not. The label had little impact on how they judged the advice. Most readers seemed to overlook the AI label entirely. The result suggests labels may not alter trust as expected.

dig.q: Will AI labels affect other types of content?
How can we make AI disclosures more noticeable?
What ethical rules should guide AI‑generated information?

stories.headline: New Experiments Chase Elusive Ultralight Dark Matter
stories.body: Scientists are creating fresh experiments to look for ultralight dark matter, a type of invisible material thought to make up most of the universe’s mass. These experiments use clever techniques that can detect tiny vibrations or energy shifts caused by the particles. By expanding the search methods, researchers hope to catch signals that older tools missed. Finding ultralight dark matter would help explain why galaxies spin faster than visible matter alone can account for.
stories.aha: Detecting ultralight dark matter could finally reveal the hidden mass that holds galaxies together.

stories.headline: Two Childhood Stages Most Sensitive to Screen Time
stories.body: Researchers have pinpointed two age windows when screen exposure can hurt learning and memory the most: early infancy and the beginning of school. Children who spend more time on screens during these periods later show lower grades and weaker working memory. The study links heavy screen use to lasting impacts on academic performance years after the exposure. Parents and teachers can use this information to limit screen time during these critical stages.
stories.aha: Limiting screens in infancy and early school years protects kids’ long‑term learning ability.

stories.headline: Rare Triple-Star System Defies Stellar Theory
stories.body: Astronomers have accidentally discovered a nearby triple-star system named Welopō'ai that should not exist according to current models. The system contains a red dwarf star tightly orbiting two dense white dwarfs, the remnants of dead stars. Normally, when the original star became a white dwarf, it would have swallowed the red dwarf, but the red dwarf survived. This odd arrangement forces scientists to rethink how close‑orbiting stars evolve.
stories.aha: A surviving red dwarf near two white dwarfs shows stars can survive explosions we thought would destroy them.

stories.headline: AI Tools Redefine Work of Theoretical Physicists
stories.body: Cutting‑edge artificial intelligence programs are now solving physics problems that once required a day of work by top researchers. These AI systems can crunch equations, test hypotheses, and suggest new models at lightning speed. As a result, the daily tasks of theoretical physicists are shifting from manual calculations to guiding and interpreting AI output. The change promises faster discoveries but also raises questions about the future role of human scientists.
stories.aha: AI can now do a physicist’s day‑long calculations in minutes, reshaping the field.

stories.headline: Treasure Hunt Fuels Fierce Shipwreck Battles
stories.body: For centuries, the wreckage of lost ships has sparked violent contests over who can claim the sunken cargo. Salvagers, governments, and treasure hunters often fought each other, sometimes using legal tricks or force to secure rights. The high value of recovered goods turned shipwreck sites into lucrative, cut‑throat markets. Understanding this history shows how the lure of treasure can drive intense competition on the high seas.
stories.aha: Shipwrecks have long been a battlefield where treasure drives ruthless competition.
